fields.title: Somalia - El Niño flood risk in displacement sites (September 2026)
fields.body:
**Key message**

Despite widespread and recurrent flooding, evacuations remained limited: 83% of sites flooded at least once between 2023 and 2025, while only 15% to 21% of flooded sites reported evacuations in any given year.

98% of the assessed sites reported living in a buul or transitional shelter. These are structures that flooding might destroy rather than merely dampen.

**Context**

Somalia's 2023 Deyr floods affected 2.5 million people and displaced 1.2 million, with around 118 deaths reported.1 A post-disaster assessment across 16 districts put damage and losses at US$193.4 million.2 Similar causal factors underlying that crisis are present this year: El Niño conditions are now rated at 100% probability through early 2027, with many models projecting a very strong event peaking during the Deyr rainy season, coinciding with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole.3 ICPAC gives a 90% chance of elevated October–December rainfall over central and southern Somalia.4 FEWS NET expects September–November rainfall above 120% of average and flags a risk of famine in parts of the south if flooding is extreme, in a context already strained by persistent drought and erratic 2026 Gu rains.5 The Deyr rains begin in October, leaving a narrow window for preparedness. Between June and July 2026, Acted and DRC assessed 412 IDP sites across 13 districts to establish how those sites fared in 2023–2025 and what capacity to evacuate exists today.

fields.title: Tchad : Evaluation territoriale et Plan de relèvement local d’Adré - Octobre 2026
fields.body:
**RESUME EXECUTIF**

Frontalière du Darfour, la sous-préfecture d’Adré est l’une des zones de l’est du Tchad les plus affectées par la crise soudanaise, avec 214 943 réfugiés enregistrés à la date du 14 septembre 2026,1 et une place parmi les dix premières zones accueillant des retournés vulnérables en juillet 2026.2 Les informations disponibles y restaient fragmentées et peu centrées sur l’ensemble des groupes de populations – déplacés et non-déplacés – présents à l’échelle territoriale. Pour y remédier, une évaluation territoriale (ABA) a été conduite dans le cadre de l’initiative AGORA, financée par l’Agence Française pour le Développement (AFD), avec l’implication du Comité Mixte de Gouvernance Territoriale (CMGT) mis en place par la même initiative, afin d’appuyer la planification locale et l’élaboration d’une feuille de route opérationnelle dénommée Plan de Relèvement Local (PRL).

L’évaluation couvre la Ville d’Adré, le site d’accueil temporaire (SAT) et 42 villages situés dans un rayon d’environ 20 km. Elle combine des données quantitatives et qualitatives collectées d’avril à août 2026 avec une composante d’analyse géospatiale transversale : cartographie des infrastructures et des cartographies participatives, analyses d’accessibilité aux services, télédétection (occupation du sol, stress de la végétation), modélisation des zones inondables et tendances climatiques sur 30 ans. Elle permet de spatialiser les résultats et d’ancrer les priorités du PRL dans le territoire. Les résultats ménages sont représentatifs pour les non-déplacés et les retournés de la Ville et pour les réfugiés du SAT ; ils sont indicatifs pour les réfugiés en Ville, comme les données rurales, qualitatives et issues des gestionnaires. L’enquête ménages, menée en saison sèche juste après le Ramadan, ne couvre pas le milieu rural

fields.title: Fiche d’information : Groupe de travail d’analyse de crises et qualité de réponse (GTACQ) Analyse provinces du Sud-Kivu, Nord-Kivu et Ituri (Août 2026)
fields.body:
**Messages clés**

- Nord-Kivu : Diminution de 10 à 8 hotspots entre juillet et août. Toutefois, cette baisse ne traduisait pas une amélioration de la situation générale mais un déplacement de la pression humanitaire vers des zones de santé telles qu’Itebero, Masisi, Pinga, Katoyi et Kibirizi qui constituaient les principaux lieux de concentration des besoins.
- Sud-Kivu : La dégradation de la situation humanitaire se traduisait par une recomposition et une extension des zones de pression. À Fizi, Minova et Kaniola, les besoins, les mouvements de population et les gaps de réponse restaient particulièrement significatifs, malgré certaines améliorations du contexte et de l’accès humanitaire.
- Ituri : une extension et une intensification de la pression humanitaire, portée à la fois par la dégradation de l’accès à Tchomia et Mongbalu et par l’aggravation des besoins et des gaps de réponse à Boga.

source.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

fields.title: Mozambique National Institute for Disaster Risk Reduction Management - Joint multisectoral assessment of potential sites/areas for the relocation of people affected by the 2026 floods (Period: 29 June to 3 July 2026) [EN/PT]
fields.body:
**Executive Summary**

The multisectoral mission assessed 14 potential relocation sites, including 12 sites previously identified by the Government and 2 identified by local communities, across the districts of Bilene, Chókwè, Guijá, Massingir, and Chibuto. The assessment was conducted by teams comprising representatives from Government institutions, humanitarian clusters, United Nations partners, and non-governmental organizations. The methodology combined direct and indirect observation, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and the use of multisectoral assessment checklists. The findings enabled the classification of sites according to their suitability for relocation, the identification of priority investments, and the development of recommendations to support the implementation of pathways towards sustainable solutions.

fields.title: Haiti: Evaluation Rapide Multisectorielle (ERM) 20260915_ACT_AVS_VIO_SMA - Localité: Almadère, Dalouet, Fouquete, Le Canta, Morne Lecanta, Morne Sale, Nan Da, Nan Pol, Nan Roger | Centre-Ville,1re,7e sections | Saint-Michel de l'Attalaye | Artibonite | 1r
fields.body:
**Aperçu du choc et contexte**

  
Le 15 septembre 2026, des membres du GCO de Savien ont mené une incursion  
armée dans la localité de Nan Paul, située dans la 7ᵉ section communale de Marmont,  
à Saint-Michel de l’Attalaye. L’attaque, survenue un jour de marché, a provoqué un  
mouvement de panique généralisé parmi les habitants et les commerçants. Après  
avoir ouvert le feu à Nan Paul, les assaillants se sont dirigés vers la localité de Bijon.  
Selon les informations recueillies, l’incident a fait une personne tuée et trois blessés  
parmi la population civile.

  
Cette attaque a entraîné des déplacements de population vers plusieurs localités de  
Saint-Michel de l’Attalaye ainsi que vers les communes d’Ennery et des Gonaïves, où  
les personnes affectées ont cherché refuge dans des zones jugées plus sûres.

source.name: Agency for Technical Cooperation and Development

fields.title: Haiti: Evaluation Rapide Multisectorielle (ERM) 20260910_ACT_AVS_VIO_STM_STM_VER - Localité: Babe, Banique, Barbe, Bois L'état, Charrette, Colmini, Dipson, Lalouere, Pont Bambou, Timonette, Zeldwat, Venotte | 4e, 5e , 6e sections | Saint-Marc | Artibonite
fields.body:
**Aperçu du choc et contexte**

Du 10 au 11 septembre, une attaque armée a été perpétrée dans la 4ᵉ section communale de Saint-Marc, plus précisément dans la localité de Robert. Au cours de cet incident, des incursions ont également été signalées dans les localités de Bel-Air, Dimany, Vielot et Dijon, situées dans la même section communale, ainsi qu’à Okabre, dans la 5ᵉ section de Bastien, commune de Verrettes.

Plusieurs maisons ont été pillées et certaines incendiées. Du bétail et des motocyclettes auraient également été volés lors de l’attaque. Plusieurs centaines de personnes auraient quitté précipitamment leur domicile à la recherche d’un lieu plus sûr.

Ces mouvements de population suscitent des préoccupations quant à la sécurité des personnes affectées ainsi qu’à leurs besoins humanitaires, notamment en matière de protection, d’hébergement et d’assistance.

La majorité des personnes déplacées auraient trouvé refuge auprès de proches ou de familles d’accueil dans différentes localités des 4ᵉ, 5ᵉ et 6ᵉ sections communales de Saint-Marc, ainsi qu'à Verrettes, où le Consortium RRM n'a pas pu mener l'ERM.

source.name: Agency for Technical Cooperation and Development

fields.title: The distance between care and access: GBV survivors in Uganda's refugee settlements’ struggle to reach life-saving support
fields.body:
## **Executive summary**

For women and girls living in Uganda’s refugee settlements, reaching life-saving support after gender-based violence can be difficult. DRC assessments in Imvepi, Lobule and Rhino Camp show how displacement, economic insecurity, unsafe movement and limited services can increase exposure to GBV while also making it harder for survivors to seek help.

Fear of being identified as a survivor is one of the biggest barriers to accessing health and psychosocial support. Distance, stigma, concerns about confidentiality, language barriers, and fear of retaliation can further delay access to care. For survivors of sexual violence, these delays can have serious consequences, as HIV post-exposure prophylaxis can only be administered within 72 hours of an assault.

The report also highlights significant differences between settlements, with services weaker and less accessible in Lobule and Rhino Camp than in Imvepi. Strengthening safe spaces, psychosocial support, and referral pathways, alongside essential health, legal, safety, and shelter services, is critical to ensuring survivors can access the support they need when they need it.

fields.title: Somali Cash Consortium - Baseline and Endline Findings MPCA Outcomes from the Direct Nutrition Referral Approach: Kismayo & Banadir, Somalia (June 2026)
fields.body:
**KEY MESSAGES**

• The use of consumption-based coping strategies declined. The proportion of households with high reduced Coping Strategy Index (rCSI) decreased sharply, from 47% to 2%, while low or medium rCSI increased to 87%. While the proportion of HHs relying on emergency, crisis or stress livelihood coping strategies (LCS) declined, a substantial share continued to rely on these strategies at endline, including 42% using emergency LCS, highlighting continued pressure on livelihoods despite improvements in food consumption.

• HH income and expenditures increased, with the largest share spent on food and medical expenses. However, most HHs still relied mainly on casual labour and humanitarian assistance as their primary source of income. Despite this improvement, HHs with debt remained widespread. More than three-quarters of assessed HHs (83%) reported having debt at endline, although the average debt burden declined from USD 84.51 at baseline to USD 70.42 at endline.

• Findings indicate that HHs remained highly financially vulnerable, with limited ability to build savings, despite improvements in income and a modest reduction in debt levels. The proportion of HHs with any savings fell sharply from 13% at baseline to just 3% at endline, while average savings declined from USD 3.32 to USD 1.89.

fields.title: Somali Cash Consortium - Baseline and Endline Findings MPCA Outcomes from the Camp Coordination and Camp Management Approach: Baidoa, Somalia (May 2026)
fields.body:
**KEY MESSAGES**

• Household (HH) expenditure increased between baseline and endline, with food and food-related debt repayment accounting for the largest shares of spending. This pattern is consistent with the prevailing context of prolonged drought and severe food insecurity, with Baidoa classified as IPC Phase 4 (Emergency) at the time of data collection. In this context, HHs were likely allocating a greater proportion of their available resources to meeting immediate food needs and repaying food-related debt. Although 83% of assessed HHs reported expenditure above the Minimum Expenditure Basket (MEB), this increase likely reflects HHs' efforts to meet essential food needs amid constrained livelihoods and heightened food insecurity, rather than an improvement in overall economic wellbeing.

• Cash assistance likely improved food security and reduced foodrelated coping strategies. Acceptable Food Consumption Score (FCS) increased from 9% at baseline to 79% at endline. While poor FCS declined from 81% to 1%. Moreover, the use of high reduced coping strategies decreased from 57% to 1%, suggesting that the cash assistance contributed to improved food access and reduced reliance on coping strategies.

• HHs employing crisis livelihood coping strategies increased from 6% to 36%, suggesting that improvements in immediate food consumption are being achieved at the cost of long-term resilience. This sharp increase suggests that many HHs continue to face substantial pressures in meeting their basic needs and are increasingly resorting to coping mechanisms that can undermine their livelihoods and future resilience.

fields.title: Sudan | Joint Market Monitoring Initiative (JMMI) Market Overview, 6 - 15 August 2026)
fields.body:
**KEY FINDINGS**

• The national Minimum Expenditure Basket (MEB) without top-up increased by 8% compared to July (689,341 SDG), reaching 746,869 SDG. The highest observed values were recorded in North Kordofan state (982,729 SDG), North Darfur state (875,178 SDG), and West Kordofan state (867,914 SDG). At the district level, the highest Total MEB values (without top-up) were observed in Sheikan, North Kordofan (1,221,786 SDG), Reifi Nahr Atbara, Kassala (1,157,293 SDG), and Tendalti, White Nile (1,000,585 SDG).

• The median cost of food items in the national MEB registered an increase of 16% from July (359,106 SDG), reaching 418,347 SDG. This is driven by a price increase of some key food items, notably, vegetable oil (+43%), goat meat (+43%), cow meat (+36%), onions (+19%), sorghum (+18%), and milk (+2%). The most expensive food components in the MEB were recorded in Um Kadadah, North Darfur (619,630 SDG) and At Tawisha, North Darfur (591,672 SDG).

• The national MEB household items without top-up decreased by 3% since July (153,125 SDG), reaching 148,167 SDG, driven by a decrease in the price of water supply (-6%), despite increases in the prices of water containers (+31%), gas refills (+8%) and gas cylinders (+5%). The highest-cost household items without top-up in the MEB were observed in Reifi Nahr Atbara, Kassala (602,000 SDG), Sheikan, North Kordofan (544,000 SDG) and Tendalti, White Nile and Um Rawaba, North Kordofan (292,000 SDG).

• The median cost of hygiene items in the national MEB recorded a 5% increase since July (61,463 SDG), reaching 64,708 SDG. This is driven by a price increase of some key items, notably, laundry soap (+26%) and body soap (+6%). The highest hygiene item costs were recorded in Kadugli, South Kordofan (117,762 SDG), Habila, West Darfur (93,776 SDG) and Al Fashaga, Gedaref (91,941 SDG).

• Overall, markets were found to be functional, with 2 localities (out of 57) recording a market functionality score below average (less than 50 out of 100), notably in Delami and Dilling (both at 43) in South Kordofan state. Additionally, more than half of the assessed localities (59%) scored below average in the resilience pillar, indicating challenges in the supply chain and restocking.

fields.title: Afghanistan: Effect of fertilizer prices on input access and product expectations - DIEM-Monitoring, August 2026
fields.body:
**Synopsis (short abstract)**

The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) conducted the twelfth round of Data in Emergencies Monitoring (DIEM-Monitoring) household-level data collection in Afghanistan from 26 April to 31 May 2026. This brief uses data from the twelfth round of DIEM-Monitoring, complemented by findings from an FAO report. Both sources provide evidence of the potential negative consequences of the ongoing Strait of Hormuz crisis for smallholder farmers, particularly through the effects of fertilizer prices on access to inputs and production expectations.The ongoing Strait of Hormuz crisis has disrupted supply chains and affected the livelihoods of resource-poor agricultural households. The anticipated effects of El Niño may create additional challenges, although the phenomenon is typically beneficial to crop production in Afghanistan. Through its extensive DIEM-Monitoring datasets, geospatial capacities and regular data collection, DIEM is well placed to analyse the effects of the crisis and monitor how El Niño may influence agricultural production and food security.

source.name: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

fields.title: République Démocratique du Congo: Évaluation à la suite d’aléas climatiques à Kamango (Août 2026)
fields.body:
**1. Contexte**

L’est de la République démocratique du Congo (RDC) demeure fortement exposé à une combinaison complexe de crises humanitaires, environnementales et sécuritaires. Dans le territoire de Beni, au Nord-Kivu, la chefferie des Watalinga est une zone largement rurale où les moyens de subsistance reposent notamment sur l’agriculture, y compris les cultures vivrières et les cultures de rente telles que le cacao et le café. La zone est également régulièrement exposée aux aléas climatiques. Son relief vallonné et ses nombreux cours d’eau exposent également certaines localités aux inondations.

Le 18 avril 2026, la chefferie des Watalinga a été touchée pendant plusieurs heures par de fortes pluies, accompagnées localement de vents violents, entraînant des ruissellements importants, des crues et débordements de cours d’eau ainsi que des dommages aux habitations, aux infrastructures et aux cultures (alerte N° 6434).

Selon les premières informations recueillies auprès des partenaires locaux, environ 521 habitations ont été endommagées et 2 045 ménages identifiés comme ayant des besoins urgents dans plusieurs localités des trois groupements de la chefferie1 . Les fortes pluies et les vents violents auraient duré une journée, tandis que l’écoulement et le passage des eaux se seraient prolongés entre deux et cinq jours selon les zones. Les déplacements et perturbations qui en ont résulté ont toutefois duré de manière variable selon les ménages, certaines familles restant encore déplacées plusieurs mois après l’événement, faute de moyens suffisants pour reconstruire et reprendre leurs activités. Des dommages ont également été signalés sur les cultures et les infrastructures, ainsi que des perturbations de l’axe routier Kamango-Bugando.

Compte tenu de l’ampleur et de la diversité des impacts rapportés, REACH et ARCEC2 ont mis en œuvre une évaluation environnementale rapide combinant enquêtes ménages, entretiens qualitatifs, observations de terrain et exercices de cartographie rapide. Réalisée du 10 au 15 août 2026, l’évaluation visait à fournir des informations opportunes et exploitables sur l’étendue des dommages, les besoins humanitaires prioritaires, ainsi que les principaux facteurs de vulnérabilité et les capacités d’adaptation des communautés face aux aléas environnementaux récurrents dans la zone de Kamango.

**Messages clés**

• Les fortes pluies et les inondations ont provoqué d’importants déplacements et dommages aux habitations. La moitié des ménages affectés a quitté leur domicile et 86% ont rapporté des dommages. Quarante-cinq pourcent des ménages déplacés étaient retournés au moment de la collecte de données (environ quatre mois après le choc), malgré des logements souvent encore inhabitables.

• Les impacts ont affecté simultanément l’accès aux services essentiels et les conditions de santé. Tous les ménages ont signalé au moins un obstacle à l’accès aux soins, 46% ont rapporté un problème de santé depuis les aléas et 82% une détresse psychologique au moins occasionnelle. Les difficultés d’accès à l’eau et à l’assainissement, ainsi que des dommages aux structures de santé et aux écoles, ont renforcé ces vulnérabilités.

• Les moyens de subsistance et la sécurité alimentaire ont été fortement affectés. 82% des ménages ayant cultivé ont signalé des impacts sur leurs cultures et 90% des difficultés à obtenir certains produits sur les marchés.

• Les capacités de préparation et d’adaptation restent limitées face à l’interaction entre aléas récurrents et vulnérabilités structurelles. 95% des ménages n’avaient reçu aucune alerte avant l’aléa et 77% n’avaient déclaré aucune des mesures d’adaptation couvertes par l’enquête. La pauvreté et la dépendance aux moyens de subsistance limitent les capacités d’adaptation et les possibilités de relocalisation, tandis que la déforestation, l’expansion du cacao sur les pentes et à proximité des cours d’eau, et la dégradation des sols contribuent à accroître l’exposition aux aléas.

fields.title: Out in the cold: Facing Winter, Facing Barriers: Assessing the Urgent Needs of Persons with Disabilities in Gaza, 2026
fields.body:
**The Humanitarian Crisis in Gaza**

Since 7 October 2023, the Gaza Strip has experienced death, destruction and mass displacement on a scale that has repeatedly overwhelmed local and international responders. According to the Ministry of Health in Gaza, as of early June 2026 more than 74,000 Palestinians had been killed and over 175,000 injured. Two million people remain displaced, many in makeshift sites with minimal access to basic services: 97% of water was deemed unfit for human consumption during 2023–2025, and around 80% of energy infrastructure had been destroyed by 2025.

The approaching winter threatens to make these conditions worse. Ahead of the 2026–27 rainy season, a joint assessment by IOM, the Site Management Cluster and the Shelter Cluster found that 989 of Gaza's 1,764 displacement sites (56%) lie in medium- or high-risk flood areas. These sites host an estimated 956,389 people, about 60% of the displaced population. Of these sites, 451 are in high-risk areas and hold more than 400,000 people who may need relocation, and 80% of all exposed sites are makeshift. Last winter's storms damaged over 42,000 tents (IOM et al., 2026).

The socioeconomic dimensions of the crisis are equally severe. According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics (PCBS, June 2026), 64 % of the Gaza Strip's population lived below the poverty line prior to the escalation; conditions have since deteriorated beyond poverty into famine, with 1.6 million people (77 % of the population) experiencing acute food insecurity as of October–November 2025, The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification. PCBS’s report 2026, estimated 58,000 children had lost one or both parents as of 18 July 2025.

This population is growing rapidly. In October 2025, the World Health Organization estimated that nearly 43,000 people had sustained life-changing injuries, about one quarter of all reported injuries. They include more than 5,000 people with amputations, who will need rehabilitation, assistive products and continued care for years. Atfaluna's community-based assessments, hearing-screening results and service data also indicate that approximately 35,000 children and adults may be at risk of temporary or permanent hearing loss. The causes include blast exposure, untreated ear injuries and infections, severe malnutrition, and the collapse of audiology and ENT services.

**Executive Summary**

As another winter of displacement approaches, persons with disabilities in the Gaza Strip are entering the rainy season in shelters that neither keep out water nor allow them to move, wash or stay warm with dignity. This assessment, conducted by Atfaluna Society for Deaf Children (ASDC) between 18 and 25 September 2026, surveyed 335 households that together include 450 persons with disabilities and 2,050 people in total.

The findings describe a population that has almost entirely lost its homes . 84% report their original home fully destroyed , and now lives predominantly in tents (75%). These tents are worn out: 58% need urgent repair and a further 18% are too cramped or obstructed for a person with a disability to move in. Only 32 households (10%) describe a shelter that is sound and wheelchair-accessible.

Winter will hit these households on several fronts at once. Nearly half (48%) already experience severe leakage that damages wheelchairs, medical mattresses and hearing aids; 95% lack sufficient blankets and clothing, and one in five (22%) resorts to open fires or charcoal inside the shelter. Four in five floors are muddy or unlevelled, 72% have no accessible toilet, and in 62% of cases flood water completely traps the person with a disability inside or outside the shelter.

Combining six of these conditions into a Winter Vulnerability Index shows that 84% of households face severe or extreme exposure, rising to 97% among families living in tents. Khan Younis and Deir al-Balah are the most affected governorates.

**Five key messages**

1\. Shelter is the first line of protection. Tarpaulins and insulation are the top-ranked need (44% rank them first priority).

2\. Warmth is not guaranteed for anyone. Only 5% have adequate blankets; clothing and blankets are the most consistently prioritised need (72% place them in their top three).

3\. Winter disables further. Mud, flooding and inaccessible toilets turn disabilities into total dependency and isolation a direct challenge to CRPD Articles 9, 19 and 20.

4\. Assistive devices are at risk. Water damages hearing aids and wheelchairs; darkness and lack of batteries cut off communication and mobility.

5\. Children are paying the price. Half of households have children under five, and 63% report rising respiratory illness in cold weather.

fields.title: Cash in transition: The State of Cash and Voucher in Syria (August 2026)
fields.body:
**Executive Summary**

Objectives: Syria’s humanitarian response is entering a period of rapid transition, while evidence on the role, effectiveness and future direction of Cash and Voucher Assistance (CVA) remains limited and fragmented. Since December 2024, changes in political authority, market access, financial services, liquidity, currency use and coordination structures have altered the conditions under which cash assistance is designed and delivered. At the same time, households continue to face severe food insecurity, weak purchasing power, debt, displacement, documentation barriers and limited livelihood opportunities. This report provides evidence on what is working, where CVA programming is constrained, and how MPCA and wider CVA can support both immediate needs and the shift towards recovery.

**Methodology:** The review is based on a mixed method approach combining secondary literature, 24 key informant interviews with CWG members, coordinators, sector actors, donors, CALP, CashCap and market experts, and analysis of programme monitoring data. The quantitative evidence includes 8,300 PDM records1, baseline and endline data, repeated PDM rounds and written monitoring reports shared by 14 I/LNGOs. The evidence base is broad and triangulated, but it should be interpreted as programme monitoring and stakeholder evidence rather than nationally representative or causal impact evidence. The data comes from different organisations, tools, locations and years, with no consistent comparison group and limited coverage of Damascus, Rural Damascus and Daraa.

**Context:** Syria continues to face a complex humanitarian crisis marked by large scale displacement, gaps in basic services, protection risks, socio economic pressures and climate shocks. Significant return movements have taken place since December 2024, but displacement remains extensive and conditions for sustainable return are uneven. Policy and funding increasingly favour return programming, but barriers remain in areas of return, including limited access to legal documentation, high living costs and limited livelihood opportunities. IDPs, returnees, women, children, older people, persons with disabilities, minorities, female headed households and camp-based households remain disproportionately affected. Food insecurity remains very high and is driven mainly by limited purchasing power rather than physical food availability. There have been modest improvements linked to remittances, lower inflation, reduced tariffs and wage increases, but humanitarian needs remain high. The report therefore recommends maintaining adequate humanitarian funding while pairing assistance more deliberately with investments in infrastructure, basic services, legal assistance, employment, livelihoods support, market systems development and other self-reliance interventions.

**CVA and MPCA Mapping:** CVA remains a central modality in Syria’s humanitarian response. In 2025, 19 percent of the implemented HRP was delivered as CVA, while 27 percent of 2026 HRP requirements represented CVA. However, MPCA accounted for only 30 percent of total CVA in 2025, and approximately 27 percent of total CVA requirements in 2026. Available data points to a potential shift away from flexible MPCA towards more sector specific CVA. Reported/delivered MPCA fell from USD 133 million in 2023 to USD 69.8 million in 2025, a 47.5 percent decrease. By contrast, broader CVA rebounded from reported USD 22 million in 2024 to USD 160.1 million in 2025, mainly reflecting the increase in sectoral cash for food. The report recognises that this shift is understandable where sectors need to meet defined objectives and demonstrate sectoral outcomes, but it also identifies risks, as MPCA remains one of the most relevant and most efficient modalities for households facing multiple overlapping needs. A reduced space for MPCA may limit households’ ability to make flexible expenditure decisions based on their own priorities.

**Market developments:** Between 2024 and 2026, Syria saw major changes in market openness, access, availability of goods and services, and the financial services ecosystem. Markets have generally become more open and better supplied since the December 2024 political transition, but market functionality remains fragile and increasingly constrained by affordability, liquidity and currency volatility. The temporary improvement seen in mid 2025, supported by lower prices, reduced restrictions, cheaper imports, lower tariffs and improved market access, began to reverse from late 2025 and early 2026 as inflationary pressure returned. Primary data analysis points to a better food security situation in 2025, likely influenced by lower prices and improved availability. However, Syria experienced severe liquidity shortages in 2025, particularly from late 2024 into the first quarter of 2025, which disrupted humanitarian operations, caused delays and contributed to some suspensions. The temporary authorisation of USD payments helped organisations manage liquidity shortages, protect transfer values and maintain continuity of operations.

**Macro-economic policies:** The shift back towards mandatory SYP payments in 2026 could support monetary normalisation in the long term, but without sufficient liquidity, realistic exchange rate management and clear regulatory guidance, it risks reducing beneficiary purchasing power, delaying distributions and recreating some of the constraints seen before the transition. CVA programmes delivered in SYP may therefore have reduced impact unless transfer values are regularly adjusted to offset purchasing power losses. The report finds no robust evidence that CVA has caused market distortions or price increases. Wider macroeconomic factors are identified as the main drivers of market trends. The report recommends that the CWG continue to advocate for USD as the main delivery currency for cash programmes to preserve the purchasing power of the most vulnerable households. If SYP becomes mandatory, the CWG should agree with relevant stakeholders on a process to continuously review and adjust transfer values for inflation.

**Banking and financial sector:** Syria’s financial sector remains highly constrained. Formal banking channels have not meaningfully resumed, correspondent banking remains limited and international banks continue to apply conservative risk controls. FSPs and hawalas remain central to humanitarian operations, providing liquidity, transfers and access to remittances in a context where the formal banking system is weak and trust in banks is low. However, they also involve high transaction costs and compliance challenges. Hawalas have adapted to the restrictive environment and already use stablecoins mainly as back-office treasury and settlement tools rather than direct delivery mechanisms for beneficiaries. The post 2024 transition is pushing the system towards more centralisation and stronger Damascus based regulation, including stronger Central Bank regulation, SYP payments, formal FSP licensing and stricter Know Your Customer (KYC) requirements. These requirements can exclude IDPs, returnees, people without valid documentation and other vulnerable groups. While formalisation may support future compliance and financial sector recovery, it may also reduce access where licensed providers have limited reach.

fields.title: VASyR 2024 - Executive Summary
fields.body:
**INTRODUCTION**

The Vulnerability Assessment of Syrian Refugees (VASyR) in Lebanon provides a multi-sectoral overview of Syrian refugees at the individual and household level. The 2024 assessment marks the twelfth annual survey evaluating the living conditions of Syrian refugee in the country. The contents of this report are jointly issued by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP).
